title: Waynesboro Public Schools provide free meals for the 2026-27 school year
text: WAYNESBORO, Va. (WHSV) - Waynesboro Public Schools will offer free, healthy breakfast and lunch to all students every day this school year. Waynesboro Public Schools nutrition supervisor Kelly Shomo said food insecurity is a major issue in the area. She says a large percentage of students qualify for free or reduced-price meals, making this program critical. “Food insecurity is fairly prevalent in our community here in Waynesboro, and it’s not just about hunger. It’s really about the stress of not knowing where your next meal is going to come from, and so that’s another reason that makes the community eligibility provision or offering all meals at no cost so important, because students don’t have to worry about where their next meal is going to come from,” she said. Shomo said around 2,000 students participate in this program, with no application required. “The great thing about the community eligibility provision, which is the program we participate in that allows us to offer meals at no cost to all students ... So we apply for that program, we participate in it, and all students are offered breakfast, lunch and snack,” she said. She said the Department of Education promotes the community eligibility provision and encourages schools and divisions to participate every year if they qualify. “So to qualify, basically, you have to have a certain percentage of students qualify for free or reduced price meals. And if you have that percentage, they really encourage you to participate so that all students can take advantage of the program,” she said. She later stated, “Funding is based on how many students we serve. So all of the reimbursable meals that we serve, or meals that meet the nutrition pattern, receive funding or reimbursement from the federal government or USDA, so it really varies. But that’s why we want to encourage as many students as possible to participate because they benefit from the program and it also sustains the program itself.” Waynesboro Public Schools also receives fresh produce for the cafeteria from local farmers in the area, including their most local site at their student education farm at Berkley Glenn Elementary. “And we offer that produce monthly in all of our schools through our Harvest of the Month program, and then we also receive produce and other local items through 4P Foods, which is a local food hub, and also Project Rose,” she said. She said having free, fresh and healthy food provided to students won’t only help their stomachs but also their brains. “When students are hungry, they can’t learn, and we know research has shown that students that participate in school meal programs they get some of the most nutritious meals that they’re going to receive. And students who participate in school breakfast, in particular, we know they have higher test scores. They have fewer discipline referrals, and they also have fewer tardies and absences,” she said. Shomo said she considers this a sustainable program and plans to continue helping feed students like this in the future. “When you participate in the community eligibility provision, you are put into a four-year cycle, so you’re locked in at the rate at which you were reimbursed for four years. So we are in our third year of the four years, and we will definitely participate through next school year and hope to participate beyond that as well,” she said.

title: Harrisonburg police give back-to-school road safety reminders
text: HARRISONBURG, Va. (WHSV) - For students, getting home safely from school doesn’t end when they step off the bus. Harrisonburg police say this is one of the most important times of the year to stay alert, watch for traffic and pay attention to what’s happening around you. Sergeant Wayne Westfall of the Harrisonburg Police Department said regardless of whether students are getting on or off the bus, when you see a school bus stopped, that means you need to stop as well. “And that’s whether the stop sign is out or not. If children are actually getting on or getting off the bus, you’re still required to stop if the sign was to malfunction ... The warning is typically the red flashing lights on the sign on the bus, and then as well as the signs out to tell you to stop. But if for some reason you come upon a bus that is, letting children on or letting children off, and the lights are not flashing, you still need to stop,” he said. Sergeant Westfall said there are consequences to not abiding by this law. “You can either get the criminal charge or you can get the civil charge. The criminal charge is going to put points on your record. It’s going to cost you a fine. The civil charge is an automatic $250 fine,” he said. He said during the school year there’s also an increase in traffic around Harrisonburg, which means an increase in accidents. That’s why drivers must be more cautious. Westfall said with it still being dark in the morning this time of year, drivers need to pay very close attention to their surroundings. It can become more difficult to see when someone is crossing the road. “When it’s darker out, you definitely need to make sure all your attention’s on the roadway. And one thing to think about is if your dash lights are on, if you’ve got your phone up, and that light, that light there, is going to affect your ability to see things in the dark,” he said. But parents have to do their part as well. Westfall said to make sure you’re teaching your kids how to behave properly when at the bus stop and walking to and from school. “One of the things they can teach your children is not to stand too close to the edge of the roadway when they’re waiting for the bus at the bus stop, try not to horseplay. You know, children are children; they like to play, but for not to be horseplaying too close to the roadway. And then also teach your children the same as you would teach your children to cross the road to look both ways,” he said. Westfall said students need to make sure they are also paying close attention to their surroundings on their commute to school, which meansavoiding having both headphones in your ears. If you are at a bus stop or walking to and from school but feel unsafe, Westfall said, call for help immediately. “If there’s an adult there that doesn’t make them feel unsafe, go to that adult and make them aware. The other would be you know call mom and dad, call you know older brothers, older siblings, call the police if it’s definitely making them that uncomfortable. If another person’s behavior is making them that uncomfortable, call the police,” he said. Sergeant Westfall says it’s simple: Slow down, stay alert, and be prepared to stop. Those few extra seconds of paying attention can make all the difference.

title: Generosity Watchword For Uncertain Times
text: With the new school year set to begin in under two weeks, on Aug.24, there goes the month of August from our traditional calendars. Football season will be well underway and all the trappings of what historically has been a post-Labor Day era will be proceeding. The School Board’s first meeting of the new year was held this week, characterized by a lengthy closed session and usual platitudes to the process by existing board members. While snapshot numbers will be available from opening day, official student enrollment numbers for the new school year will not be counted until the last day of September and we call await what they will show about new trends in this region. We know that rental unit costs are tilting downward, though home prices remain at record highs for now. As supplementary income sources dry up for the thousands who have been laid off from government jobs due to Trump administration politics, forced involuntary evictions are on the rise throughout the region. This portends a period of great uncertainty, and we can only hope our public officials are geared up for it. There are not the cushions needed to weather this transition and we fear that more people than usual, including of course, our kids, are going to be hurt. We hope we are wrong. A robust growth of the health care sector in the region may offset some of the cuts in government spending and the retail markets must certainly be prepared for adjustments. Not all the wonderful new restaurants in Falls Church are going to survive this period, even as we remain hopeful that government-organized initiatives, like the upcoming summer restaurant week, will help. Our citizens are challenged with high tax rates and surging real estate values and can respond only by trying to keep money local as much as possible. As for vacations, we do not yet have data to suggest whether those numbers are up for not, not yet anyway. A lot of pool parties and summer season barbecues may be substituting for expensive travel abroad, which would not be a bad thing from our point of view. We need to make sure our most needy citizens have enough to get by and that a generosity of spirit is maintained through tough times. These are factors over which we do have control and we call on this community in particular to maintain that spirit as the school year gets underway and demands for results begin to encroach. There are enough investments in schools and private entities here to pick up slack from economic stumbles, at least as long as they don’t snowball into something more serious. So please may the watchword of this season be generosity. It’s something we all need and can do after all. title: 3 Key Reforms Needed From November’s Election
text: The widely circulated but false report that was touted as one of the strongest non-electoral political moves in recent times, the new Pope Leo XIV, formerly known as the southside Chicago-born Robert Francis Prevost, was reported to have countered the hostility of Republicans in the U.S. Congress by extending a warm personal welcome to U.S. public health advocate Anthony Fauci to visit him in Rome. Sadly, the report turned out to be false in any formal sense, although Fauci did deliver key remarks at a 2021 conference in Rome led by Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis on the role of public health. Still, however, I contend that the false rumor remained true in the spiritual sense that it reflected the sentiments of a pontiff who is clearly aligned with the social movement for scientific progress and against those in theTrump administration who continue to rely on dangerous mythologies to justify policies that are killing people. Among the worst of these is Samuel Alioto, the U.S. Supreme Court justice who framed the argument used to undo the critical Roe Vs. Wade decision on the legal rights of women’s bodies. Justice Samuel Alito was forced to revert to the 13th-century English cleric, judge, and royal justice Henry de Bracton to argue that abortion restrictions have deep roots in English common law. The right to abortion has been the ardent target of key factions within the Republican Party for years. And the untimely death of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg allowed former President Donald Trump to deploy judicial appointments to deliver Roe’s execution notice in late 2020. When Justice Sonia Sotomayor pointed this out at oral argument in Dobbs, she was only stating what every single participant in the confirmation battles of the last several years well understood, and only the willfully blind could deny. He is famous for compiling De Legibus et Consuetudinibus Angliae (“On the Laws and Customs of England”), a massive and influential 13th-century legal text that blended English custom with Roman and canon law. Alito quoted Bracton’s treatise to establish historical precedent, noting the text’s assertion that if a person strikes a pregnant woman or gives her poison to cause an abortion—specifically if the fetus is “formed and animated” (quickened)—the perpetrator commits homicide. But legal historians and Bracton scholars criticized Alito’s reading. They pointed out that Bracton’s text made a sharp distinction regarding “quickening” (when movement is felt), and that medieval canon law typically treated early-stage termination through a lens of religious penance rather than secular capital murder. Critics argued that citing a medieval cleric’s ecclesiastical-influenced text misrepresents how the common law actually operated regarding reproductive autonomy before the modern era. Active during the reign of King Henry III, Bracton served as a judge on the King’s Bench and as an itinerant justice. Like many educated professionals of the Middle Ages, he was also an ordained Catholic priest holding high ecclesiastical titles, eventually becoming the chancellor of Exeter Cathedral. But it is patently absurd that an issue of vital importance to more than half the entire population has to be based on shady references to something written 800 years ago. The American revolution, after all, was fought to expel the remnants of a corrupt anti-democratic British system. So the solution to what Alito did now awaits critical reforms here that I believe need to be implemented having nothing to do with political labels but solely with justice and fair play. The reforms we need are three. Expand the Supreme Court to 14 justices, correlated to the 14 court districts of the nation, end the Electoral College and go instead to a popular vote policy, removing the fact that states like Wyoming and North Dakota have the same number of U.S. senators as California or New York, and enlarge the Congress to take population growth into account. These changes do not signal any change in our basic Constitutional system, but expand the reign of equality while removing some egregious stumbling blocks to justice. In other words, the charge of socialism need not apply at all. The post 3 Key Reforms Needed From November’s Election first appeared on Falls Church News-Press Online .

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day by Lisa Sinrod
text: The latest Spider-Man offering, rated PG-13 and released on July 31 by Sony Pictures, is a direct sequel to 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home”. The Spider-Man franchise is one of the most successful superhero film series ever made and the new film has just achieved the status of the biggest box office opening in history. Since 2002, three actors have portrayed Spider-Man in live-action films based on the Marvel Comics character. British actor Tom Holland has played Peter Parker/Spider-Man since 2016 in four standalone Spider-Man movies, including the current one, and three ensemble Marvel Cinematic Universe films. Holland, starring in this version along with Zendaya, combines youthful energy with a vulnerability that suits the iconic Spider-Man role. Peter Parker, Spider-Man’s alter ego, is a brilliant young man who uses his superhuman abilities to protect others while struggling to balance his justice missions with everyday life. Parker assumes his Spider-Man identity when his superhero abilities are needed to fight crime. Zendaya has appeared in all three of Holland’s previous Spider-Man movies as Michelle Jones-Watson (MJ), Peter Parker’s classmate and love interest. The American singer and actress is, at age 29, one of Hollywood’s most prominent young performers. There is an infectious onscreen chemistry between Zendaya and Holland (age 30). “Brand New Day” provides some background from the 2021 film, revealing that a spell cast at the end of “Spider-Man: No Way Home” caused the world to forget who Peter Parker is. Now embarking on a more solitary existence, Parker fully embraces his identity as Spider-Man, protecting New York City while living apart from his former life. Even MJ, and his best friend Ned, no longer know who he is. Parker occasionally checks on MJ by showing up where he knows she will be, to make sure she is safe. These poignant scenes underscore his longing to reconnect with her while recognizing that doing so could place her in danger. In the Spider-Man origin story, Peter Parker became Spider-Man after a genetically altered (or radioactive, depending on the version) spider bit him, giving him extraordinary abilities. These abilities include enhanced strength, agility, wall-crawling, and web-slinging. In this film, Parker experiences strange physical symptoms due to his arachnid DNA evolving. These changes make it harder for him to control his special abilities. He turns to physicist Bruce Banner, perfectly played by Mark Ruffalo, who helps him develop a DNA inhibitor to slow this process. At the same time, Spider-Man begins investigating a series of mysterious crimes involving the Department of Damage Control. As he delves into the crimes, circumstances are such that he and MJ (Zendaya’s character) cross paths. Since her memory of who he is has been erased, it is interesting watching the two interact while only Spider-Man knows of their past romantic connection. The sparks fly regardless and sets-up the question as to whether they will reunite. It was Peter, after all, who at the conclusion the 2021 film agreed with Doctor Strange’s proposal to cast a spell making everyone forget him in order to save the multiverse. During this film, Peter crosses paths with Frank Castle, known as the Punisher. They both have the goal of protecting innocent people but differ over their methods. Spider-Man refuses to kill, while Castle believes lethal force can be necessary. Jon Bernthal, a powerful character actor who grew up in this area, plays Frank Castle. As the movie unfolds, things get complicated and at times overly busy, but the film doesn’t lose its appeal. Additional characters are brought in and plot twists abound. A central theme is whether Doctor Strange’s spell was a necessary sacrifice to protect the multiverse and those closest to Parker. For Spider-Man afficionados, this film should be a welcome delight. It is currently playing on several screens at Falls Church’s own Paragon Founders Row theaters. Positive audience reaction to “Brand New Day” is noteworthy in what is currently a summer movie landscape that is unusually concentrated around just a few major releases. For the uninitiated, it can be hard to fully connect the dots on all of the moving parts of the film without having seen the recent prior versions. However, “Brand New Day” represents a new chapter in Parker’s life and is enjoyable regardless for those who have no prior Spider-Man experience (consider me the test subject on that). A post-credits scene hints at Peter’s future role in the next phase of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, so expect more sequels. title: A Penny for Your Thoughts
text: by Penny Gross Exclusive to the Falls Church News-Press Senator Ted Cruz (R-T) should be ashamed of himself. And Senators Bernie Moreno (R-OH) and Josh Hawley (R-MO), too. The vote count for the Michigan Senate primary hadn’t even been certified when Cruz appeared on FOX television to denounce Dr. Abdul El-Sayed as a communist and an Islamist, invoking the type of hate speech that was rampant in the 1950s during Joe McCarthy’s (D-WI) “Red Scare” campaign. Cruz’ reprehensible comments are part of his usual pattern, demonizing people and denigrating issues. Respectful dissension is part and parcel of being a United States Senator in either party, but the emphasis should be on the “respectful” part. Responsible discourse demands respect, a virtue missing in current debates. Respect also was in short supply when 85-year-old Dr. Anthony Fauci was summoned to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in late July about his role in the global COVID pandemic six years ago. Sensing that committee chairman Rand Paul (R-KY) was setting a potential perjury trap, Dr. Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment protections to every question, including cheeky questions from Senator Hawley about the day of the week, the color of his tie, the carpet, etc. Hawley wasn’t seeking answers; he was performing for the television cameras, using Dr. Fauci as his foil. It was a shameful episode with a brash younger man berating a renowned scientist almost twice his age, several times referring to Dr. Fauci informally as “Doc.” While Hawley’s routine was condescending and loud, Senator Moreno’s comments at the Fauci hearing were crude and vulgar. Maybe Moreno hasn’t been a Senator long enough to learn the rules of Senate decorum, but using four-letter words (f-bombs and s-words) in official Senate proceedings is a no-no. Had he uttered those words on the Senate Floor instead of a committee hearing, he might have been called out by other Senators for his use of language, and his words “taken down” (taken out of the written Congressional Record). In the late 1950s, Senator Wayne Morse (D-OR) termed Senator Homer Capehart (R-IN), who was rather portly, a “tub of rancid ignorance” about some long-distant disagreement. That comment on the Senate Floor elicited a brief tempest, but no rebuke to the maverick from Oregon who was well-known for his mastery of language and forceful comments, almost always said with a measure of respect for the audience or the witness. Like it or not, election to public office automatically confers leadership responsibility. Election makes you a role model, especially for young people. Elected officials who squander the opportunity and responsibility may get some notoriety and more “clicks” temporarily, but the broader impact is on political attitudes and society in a race to the bottom. The only political context for many younger people has been the past ten years or so, as Donald Trump has coarsened the political dialogue and made lies and vilification – of women, the press, immigrants, disabled persons, other nations – the everyday coinage of his regime. Is it any wonder, then, that chaos and disrespect have become normalized in lieu of the respect and decorum that should govern discourse as well as disagreement? Senators Cruz, Moreno and Hawley should look in the mirror and ask, “Am I a good role model for children?” That would be a useful question to ask ourselves, too. title: Our Man In Arlington 8-13-2026
text: What is the difference between the police department and the sheriff’s office? That is a complicated question, due to the evolution of Virginia’s local governments. The short answer to this question is that the police department falls under the control of the county, and the sheriff’s office is subject to the control of the state. As for the long answer, let’s start with a little history, taking you back to 17 th century Virginia. In 1634, the Colony of Virginia was divided into eight shires (a fancy British word for counties). The shire form of government included the appointed position of sheriff. In England, the “High Sheriff” collected royal taxes, managed the king’s estates, kept the peace, and ran local courts (surely you remember the Sheriff of Nottingham from various Robin Hood movies). Following the American Revolution, the Governor of Virginia appointed sheriffs for fixed terms. The Virginia Constitution of 1830 shifted the office, making the sheriff an elected position in the counties and cities. Sheriffs handled all law enforcement roles, but by the late 19 th century, some cities created separate police departments. The City of Alexandria had the first police department, starting in 1870. In the early 20 th century, Arlington County’s laws were enforced by one sheriff, one deputy sheriff, and about twelve special officers whose job was to patrol one of the fastest-growing counties in America. The population grew from 6,430 in 1900 to 57,040 in 1940. Arlington’s proximity to the District of Columbia made it a haven for gamblers, and for bootleggers during Prohibition. Arlington’s sheriff’s office was made up of men whose method of operation had not changed since the early 1900’s. They were not paid salaries; instead, they earned money for every arrest made or warrant served. At a time when much of Arlington still had no indoor plumbing, the deputy sheriffs supplemented their income by being paid to inspect the county’s outhouses. The long-time elected sheriff, Howard Fields, was a bit of a character (or caricature might be the better word). As recounted in an interview with long-time Arlington attorney Tom Phillips,Sheriff Fields was the picture of a small-town sheriff – a slightly overweight man in his middle 50’s, just under six feet tall, with an imposing walrus mustache. Fields never carried a gun but used “the strength of his personality and a poison-eyed stare” to enforce the county’s laws. By 1939, Sheriff Fields realized a change was needed. In a letter to the county board in January of 1940, Fields stated, “Because of the growth of the county … I agree with the general trend of public opinion that there should be a change in the police set-up and would like to request that the administration of the police department, including the recommendation of men for appointment thereto, be transferred to the county manager.” A separate county police department was formed on February 1, 1940, with nine officers. I hesitate to make this summary of law enforcement responsibilities more confusing, but I must add that the stories of other Virginia jurisdictions can be even more bewildering. Loudoun County has a sheriff’s office, but no police department. Some cities have sheriffs and a police department, and some cities have only a police department. Some cities have jails, while other cities rely on using county jails. But let me circle back to my original question: What is the difference between the police department and the sheriff’s office? The most succinct answer lies in their mission statements. The mission of the Arlington County Police Department is “… the reduction of the incidence of crime and the improvement of the quality of life in Arlington County by making it a place where all people can live safely and without fear.” The mission of the Arlington County Sheriff’s Office is “…to make the justice system work, and foster Commitment, Diversity, Integrity, Respect, and Teamwork.” What comprises this “justice system”? Next week I will explain this term and write about the main duties of the sheriff’s office. The post Our Man In Arlington 8-13-2026 first appeared on Falls Church News-Press Online .

title: Extraordinary Hearts Book Review
text: Let’s get off on the right foot: this is a rave review. Nick Benton’s newly updated third edition of Extraordinary Hearts (BCI Books, Falls Church) is an ambitious, provocative, and deeply personal work that deserves a wide readership. While readers may disagree with some of its arguments—and Benton occasionally presses his case with unmistakable polemical zeal—the book is a significant contribution to the ongoing conversation about LGBTQ history, culture, and the forces that have shaped civilization. Best known as the publisher and editor of the Falls Church News-Press since 1991, Benton brings to this volume the perspective of a seasoned journalist, social observer, and lifelong advocate. The third edition revisits and expands essays written over many years, presenting a comprehensive statement of his philosophy concerning what he calls the “gay sensibility” and its enduring influence from classical Greece to the modern era. The book’s subtitle, Reclaiming Gay Sensibility’s Central Role in the Progress of Civilization , signals the breadth of Benton’s ambitions. His argument ranges across philosophy, literature, politics, religion, and history, connecting figures as diverse as Socrates, Plato, Walt Whitman, Oscar Wilde, Tennessee Williams, and E.M. Forster. Whether readers ultimately embrace all of his conclusions or not, Benton consistently challenges conventional assumptions and invites serious engagement. One of the book’s central themes is the distinction Benton draws between two competing visions of love. On one side is a higher, civic-minded ideal rooted in justice, creativity, compassion, and the advancement of society. On the other is a more narrowly individualistic pursuit of pleasure detached from a broader ethical purpose. This framework provides the intellectual backbone for much of the book and gives coherence to its wide-ranging historical discussions. Among the most compelling sections is Benton’s treatment of E.M. Forster. He recalls Forster’s celebrated injunction in Howards End to “Only connect,” linking it to the author’s later essay “What I Believe” and its vision of “an aristocracy of the sensitive, the considerate and the plucky.” Benton argues that Forster’s appeal was never simply about romance or physical intimacy but about bridging the divide between intellect and emotion, private fulfillment and public responsibility. If the book has a weakness, it is that its sweeping historical claims occasionally move faster than some readers may wish. There are moments when Benton states broad conclusions with greater confidence than the available evidence may persuade every skeptical reader to accept. Yet even where one questions his conclusions, the arguments are thoughtful, passionately presented, and intellectually engaging. That is ultimately the achievement of Extraordinary Hearts . It is not content merely to recount LGBTQ history; it seeks to reinterpret it and to place it at the center of the larger story of human progress. Whether one agrees with every aspect of Benton’s thesis or not, the book rewards careful reading and reflection. It is an important work by one of Northern Virginia’s most distinctive journalistic voices, and one well worth adding to the conversation. title: Shenandoah County School Board votes to appeal federal ruling over Confederate school names
text: SHENANDOAH COUNTY, Va. (WHSV) - The Shenandoah County School Board voted unanimously on Thursday night to appeal a federal judge’s ruling ordering the county to remove confederate school names from two public schools. The board voted 6-0 to retain appellate counsel and pursue an appeal of the final order and judgement issued Aug. 6 by the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia. The case involves the Virginia State Conference NAACP and others versus the Shenandoah County School Board. A federal judge ruled the school board violated students’ rights when it restored the names of two schools in 2024. The board’s resolution authorizes appellate counsel to file a notice of appeal, seek a stay or other relief while the appeal is pending and take other necessary actions to pursue the appeal. Board Vice Chair Whitney Pence said the board believes it has a responsibility to examine the federal courts decision. “When a federal court’s remedy reaches directly into that local decision-making authority, I believe this board has every right and a responsibility to carefully examine whether that solution is legally justified and whether review by appeals is appropriate,” Pence said. The motion was made by Pence and seconded by Michael D. Rickard. The resolution was approved unanimously by the board.

text: The National Park Service announced the planned interment of a Civil War soldier recovered during archaeological excavations at Manassas National Battlefield Park. Based on the analysis, the soldier likely fought in the Second Battle of Manassas in August of 1862 and he was approximately 16-19 years old. The planned transfer to Arlington National Cemetery reflects the National Park Service’s dual responsibility to preserve and study archaeological resources while treating human remains with dignity and respect. National Park Service Superintendent Kristofer Butcher said, “Every soldier who fought on this battlefield has a story, even if we may never know their name. During staffed hours, customers can shop with Lori’s Gifts employees. But when staff members are not present, shoppers can enter using a credit or debit card, phone or smartwatch and pay for the items they take. Angie Dritto, manager of Lori’s Gifts at Augusta Health, said the new model also provides more flexibility for employees while ensuring the store remains available to the hospital. “When our staff is not here for you, there’s a gate, and you’ll use your credit card, debit card, tap pay with your phone or smartwatch,” Dritto said. “Once you come in, whatever items you take with you is what you’re charged.” Augusta Health has partnered with Lori’s Gifts for more than a decade. Todd Lilley, the executive sponsor of the project, said the idea was developed to provide patients, families and hospital employees with more amenities, particularly during evenings and overnight hours. “If you’re a family member, that’s just waiting to get information, and you’re here in the emergency department, are you here waiting for tests? Even if you’re waiting for a prescription, [if] you just have a moment that you can come and look around and browse, maybe find something that you need.” Lilley said the expanded offerings go beyond traditional convenience items. Customers can now purchase freshly made sandwiches, fresh flowers and freshly brewed Starbucks coffee. Lilley adds the transition to Go Market by Lori’s is part of an effort to make the hospital experience more convenient and comfortable for patients, visitors and staff.

title: Red Cross urges blood donors as crisis continues
text: HARRISONBURG, Va. (WHSV) - The American Red Cross says the nation remains in a blood crisis as donations continue to fall short of demand. The organization reported a roughly 25% drop in the nation’s blood supply in June, prompting the Red Cross to declare a blood crisis. Khristopher Dumschat, Virginia regional communications manager with the American Red Cross, said the organization has seen an increase in blood donations in parts of Virginia, including the Harrisonburg area. “We’ve definitely seen, especially in the different areas of Virginia, especially the Harrisonburg area, we have seen an increase in people coming up, coming out to donate blood at our various blood drives” Dumschat added, “That does not mean that we’re out of a crisis or shortage at this time, but we definitely, have seen people answer the call, uh, and do something really amazing Despite the increase in donations, Dumschat said the blood supply has not recovered enough to end the crisis. The Red Cross is encouraging eligible donors to schedule an appointment. People can visit RedCrossBlood.org and enter their ZIP code to find nearby blood drives. Donors can also use the Red Cross Blood Donor App to find drives and complete a RapidPass before their appointment to help speed up check-in. Dumschat said there is a particular need for O-positive blood, which hospitals can use in emergencies. Anyone healthy and eligible to donate is encouraged to schedule an appointment and help replenish the nation’s blood supply.

title: VDH discusses the most common diseases in VA, as some cases continue to rise
text: HARRISONBURG, Va. (WHSV) -Health officials are keeping an eye on several infectious diseases across Virginia, from respiratory illnesses and foodborne infections to tick-borne diseases and sexually transmitted infections. While some of these illnesses are more common than others, the Virginia Department of Health said knowing how they spread and how to prevent them can help keep you and your family healthy. Rachel Dumene said that, with school starting back up, it’s even more important to pay attention to which diseases could be passed around. “With back to school time happening right now, we can really expect those rates of respiratory illnesses to rise, just because so many people are going to be back in settings where there’s a lot of people gathered indoors for a long amount of time, and that would include things like the flu, COVID-19, and then pertussis.” In VDH’s most recent study from 2024, these are the top infectious diseases reported in Virginia, with congenital syphilis being one that’s started to make its way up the chart: Chlamydia trachomatis infection 74,926 cases Gonorrhea 27,262 cases Hepatitis C, chronic 8,230 cases Campylobacteriosis 4,572 cases Syphilis, early 3,762 cases Salmonellosis (Salmonella) 3,124 cases Hepatitis B, chronic 2,906 cases Lyme disease 2,812 cases Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) 1,702 cases Pertussis (Whooping Cough) 1,654 cases Congenital syphilis is passed from mother to baby when a woman is pregnant or when she gives birth--then it can also be very harmful for a newborn baby. It can severely affect their health and have really negative impacts. So that’s something that’s rising across the entire state, and we’re seeing very concerning levels of that right now. She said people should consider getting properly screened and treated because it can be prevented. Dumene said there are a lot of different kinds of diseases, which means there are many different symptoms and different ways it can be transmitted... “Obviously, for a respiratory illness, someone coughing or sneezing or having close contact with someone else is going to highly increase the chances of someone else getting sick. There’s other things such as foodborne illness that might not necessarily spread person to person, but could be from one contaminated source, which we’ve seen recently with a cyclosporiasis outbreak,” she said. Dumene said washing your hands, staying vaccinated and properly cleaning your food all play a huge role in keeping yourself and others healthy. “Something that people should always keep in mind for preventing foodborne illness is washing their hands thoroughly when they’re preparing food, keeping meat and produce separate from one another in preparation...as far as measles go, we have seen unfortunately a decrease in vaccination rates across the state, and sometimes pockets of unvaccinated people can be exposed to the illness. And measles is one of the most contagious illnesses that we are aware of, so it spreads very easily,” she said. The number one infectious disease on the chart is chlamydia in Virginia, with more than 74,000 cases. Dumene said she can’t stress enough the importance of getting tested, especially because some STDs don’t have any symptoms. “There are certain behaviors that carry high inherent risk of spreading disease, such as intravenous drug use or unprotected sex. And there is a program called Harm Reduction, and that primary goal is to mitigate the spread of illness with those high-risk behaviors, such as using condoms. That would be a great example of harm reduction because that helps prevent the spread of STIs between partners,” she said. She said preventing bug bites from ticks and mosquitoes is also important, as it could lead to things like Lyme disease or the dengue virus. “It’s really up to us to use proper prevention strategies to prevent any bug-borne illness from ticks or mosquitoes, and that can include things such as using bug repellent, making sure that you’re not walking around in high brush areas, just tall grass, if you can avoid it, tucking your long pants into long socks so that you can better identify ticks that are crawling on you and get them off of you before they bite you, and then doing thorough tick checks after every time you’re outside,” she said.
